name: Kiddie Tax Planning Around Child Wages

advisor.summary: The §1(g) kiddie tax pulls a covered child's net unearned income above $2,700 (2026 — two $1,350 layers) up to the parents' marginal rates, neutralizing naive gifts of income-producing assets. It never touches earned income: wages from the family business are taxed at the child's own rates and absorbed by a standard deduction that tracks earned income up to $16,100. The planning problem therefore sits downstream of payroll — wages accumulating in a taxable custodial account eventually throw off enough interest and dividends to cross the threshold and land at the parents' top rate. The discipline is sequencing: Roth IRA first, plan deferrals second, 529 third, and low-yield holdings for whatever must stay taxable. This is a guardrail strategy for families running the hire-the-kids playbook, not a standalone deduction, and it is priced accordingly.
mechanics: §1(g) reaches children under 18, 18-year-olds whose earned income covers no more than half their support, and full-time students 19–23 under the same earned-income test — substantial wages can move an older student out of scope entirely.
Net unearned income equals unearned income minus two $1,350 layers (2026, per Rev. Proc. 2025-32) — in practice, unearned income above $2,700 is taxed at the parents' rates on Form 8615.
Earned income is never kiddie-taxed and separately enlarges the child's standard deduction under §63(c)(5)(B) — wages up to $16,100 (2026) enjoy double protection.
The trap is accumulation: wages parked in a taxable custodial brokerage compound until the yield crosses $2,700, and the excess is then taxed at the parents' 32–37% instead of the child's rates.

The defusing sequence: custodial Roth IRA up to the $7,500 limit (2026, Notice 2025-67), then 401(k) deferrals where the plan permits, then 529 funding — leaving little or nothing to generate taxable yield.
Where a taxable account is unavoidable, hold low-distribution assets and schedule gain harvesting for years the child falls outside the covered-age tests.

authority.note: The kiddie tax — a covered child's net unearned income taxed at the parents' marginal rates; earned income sits categorically outside it.
The dependent standard deduction tracks earned income plus an add-on — why wages are sheltered up to $16,100 for 2026.
The computation and filing mechanics for any year the child's unearned income crosses the threshold.
The 2026 inflation figures, including the $1,350 kiddie-tax layers and the dependent standard deduction.
The 2026 IRA limit ($7,500) sizing the first leg of the wage-routing sequence.

requirements: A child with earned income from the family business (or elsewhere) and actual or planned investment assets in their name.
A complete inventory of child-titled accounts — custodial brokerage, custodial Roth, 529 — and the income each one produces.
Annual monitoring of each child's unearned income against the $2,700 threshold.
Coordination with the hire-children, kids' Roth IRA, and kids' 401(k) strategies — this strategy routes those dollars.
risks: No aggressive position needs defending here — the risk is inattention: several years of wages compounding in a taxable custodial account will eventually throw off kiddie-taxable yield at the parents' top rate, quietly clawing back the payroll strategy's benefit.

Custodial-account transfers are irrevocable — assets placed in a child's name for tax reasons cannot be reclaimed, and large custodial balances count against financial aid more heavily than parent-owned 529s.
Coverage runs to age 23 for full-time students — assuming the rule stops at 18 produces surprise Form 8615 filings in the college years.
Rebalancing appreciated custodial positions triggers gains that are themselves kiddie-taxable — dispositions belong in uncovered years.
stateNotes: Missouri conforms automatically: the Form 8615 result lands in federal AGI, the Missouri starting point (RSMo §143.121) — no separate Missouri kiddie regime exists.
No PTET interaction — this is an individual-side sequencing strategy with no entity deduction in play.

Missouri-specific: the 529 leg carries extra state value — Missouri allows a deduction of up to $8,000 per taxpayer ($16,000 MFJ) for MOST 529 contributions, stacking a state benefit on top of the federal shelter.
reviewChecklist: Account inventory current for each child, with projected interest, dividends, and planned gains tested against the $2,700 threshold.
Wage-routing order (Roth, then plan deferrals, then 529) documented and actually funded this year.
Student-age children (19–23) tested annually on the earned-income-versus-support condition.
Form 8615 prepared proactively in any year the threshold is crossed — not discovered on notice.

client.teaser: Keep your kids' money taxed at their low rates — not dragged up to yours.
client.headline: Don't let a family tax rule claw back your planning wins
plainEnglish: There is a rule nicknamed the kiddie tax. It stops parents from parking investments in a child's name to skip tax. Once a child's investment income tops $2,700 in a year, the extra is taxed at the parents' rates.
Here is the good news. Money your child earns by working — like wages from the family business — is never touched by this rule. Wages are always taxed at the child's own low rates.

So the plan is all about where the wages go next. Left in a normal investment account, they will one day earn enough interest to trip the rule. Routed into a Roth IRA, a retirement plan, or a college fund, the growth stays out of reach. We map that route for each child and check it every year.
client.analogy: Think of your child's wages as water and the accounts as buckets. Some buckets slowly leak tax back at your rates as they fill. Others are sealed tight. We fill the sealed buckets first.
benefits: Your kids' money stays taxed at their rates — or grows tax-free
No surprise bills at your top rate on their accounts
Turns family payroll into decades of protected growth
One simple yearly check, with no extra filings unless a line is crossed
steps: WE list every account in your kids' names and the income each one produces.
WE set the routing order — Roth IRA first, then retirement plan, then college fund.
YOU fund the accounts in that order as wages come in.
WE re-check the numbers each year as balances grow.
clientCommitments: Follow the funding order we set before adding to any taxable account
Tell us about new accounts or gifts in a child's name before they happen

annualMaintenance: Audit each child-titled account's yield against the kiddie-tax threshold every year
Re-run the earned-income-versus-support test for students 19–23
Update the routing plan for new wages and current-year contribution limits
deliverables: Per-child account inventory and yield projection
Wage-routing plan (Roth, plan deferrals, 529) for each child
Annual threshold memo, with Form 8615 preparation when required
